03 / BUSINESS ANALYSIS · PRODUCT REQUIREMENTS · UAT

Dezinersknot

A marketplace experience depends on more than the interface.

The work in one minute

Dezinersknot connects clients with freelance designers. But matching two people is only the beginning of a project.

Before work can move forward, both parties need to understand the requirements, agree on commercial terms, manage submissions, review deliverables, and complete payments.

My contribution focused on the decisions and operational work behind this experience: gathering feedback, clarifying requirements, analyzing alternatives, supporting payment-provider onboarding, testing functionality, and coordinating implementation across teams.

The challenge

How might we translate evolving business requirements and user expectations into a marketplace experience that is clear, operationally feasible, and ready for implementation?

The business team owned core commercial decisions. The external studio created much of the original visual UI. This page focuses on my documented contributions, not authorship of their screens.

PRODUCTTwo-sided freelance design marketplace
MY ROLEBusiness Analysis · UX refinement · UAT · provider onboarding · coordination
PERIODJan 2025–Oct 2026 · BA-focused Jul–Oct 2026
COLLABORATIONProject Manager · Business · Studio · Developers · QA · Accounts · Legal · Providers

The business team defined the core marketplace concept and owned final commercial decisions. Much of the original visual interface was produced by an external design studio. My work involved helping refine and operationalize the product through business analysis, testing, coordination and specific UX recommendations.

An illustrated story / conceptual

Two people enter one agreement with different expectations.

A client needs to define the scope and understand payment terms. A designer needs clear requirements, confidence in reviews and a workable route to payment. The product must account for both perspectives.

SCENE / 01

The opportunity

The client publishes project requirements, deliverables and budget expectations.

SCENE / 02

The negotiation

Designers submit proposals. Payment preferences and contractual expectations may differ between the parties.

SCENE / 03

The commitment

The client offers a contract. The designer can accept, propose edits or decline. Revised terms may require another decision before agreement.

SCENE / 04

The delivery

The designer submits work. The client reviews it, and approval, inactivity, disputes and payout rules determine what happens next.

01 / 04

These are editorial illustrations of documented product concepts, not historical user-research scenes or screenshots.

05 / UNDERSTANDING THE BUSINESS CHALLENGE

The difficult part was connecting decisions across the product.

The marketplace needed to support several interconnected activities, each with different requirements and stakeholders.

Client and designer preferences shaped the agreement. Financial operations constrained payment experiences. Submission and review rules affected progression, while testing exposed functionality gaps that needed clarification.

My work involved translating these requirements into actionable decisions and coordinating the teams responsible for taking them forward.

THE CONNECTED OPERATING MODEL

One journey, multiple owners and dependencies.

02 / DESIGNERProposalRespond with terms
03 / BOTHContractAgree or negotiate
04 / FINANCEPaymentFund the project
05 / DESIGNERSubmissionPresent work
06 / CLIENTReviewAccept or dispute
07 / OPERATIONSPayoutEligible release

The core challenge wasn't a single form. It was keeping business rules, responsibilities and exceptions coherent across this entire journey.

06 / FROM FEEDBACK TO PRODUCT DECISIONS

Feedback changed what the product needed to support.

Internal feedback wasn't just a list of interface changes. It helped surface product requirements that had to be analyzed, proposed, communicated to the studio and considered by development.

A / LISTENING TO USERS33

Reported internal-release participants across Microsoft Forms and direct discussions.

≈ 21

B / REQUIREMENT TRADE-OFF

One full payment isn't the same experience as one milestone.

Feedback raised the need for a distinct lump-sum payment arrangement. Representing it as one milestone was a potentially simpler engineering option, but it didn't match how people understand full-project and staged funding.

The selected product direction differentiated the two arrangements. My contribution was feedback gathering, requirements analysis and evaluating the trade-off, not authorship of the payment UI.

07 / BUSINESS RULES & EXCEPTION PATHS

What happens when the ideal workflow doesn't happen?

A marketplace must also handle cancellations, inactivity, disagreements, refunds and disputes. These are product requirements with operational and sometimes regulatory consequences.

A / PRODUCT SCOPE

From a broad wallet to refund-related credits.

A wallet-like feature raised regulatory and operational concerns. I recommended reconsidering the general-purpose stored-value model and restricting credits to refund-related use, subject to legal and business evaluation.

Reported recommendation. Specific regulatory interpretation, approval and production status require verification.

₹?
WIDER PROPOSALGeneral wallet balanceBroader fund-handling obligations
RECONSIDER SCOPE
RECOMMENDED CONSTRAINTRefund-only creditsRestricted intended use
B–C / SUBMISSION, INACTIVITY & DISPUTES

Submission is a milestone. Review is a decision.

Work can be submitted while a client is inactive or disputes the result. I worked on proposed review and exception rules, including a seven-day inactivity condition and a fourteen-day period whose exact trigger still needs confirmation.

08 / PAYMENTS & FINANCIAL OPERATIONS

A payment experience must work beyond the checkout screen.

Provider choice, bank compatibility, corporate documentation and payout operations set limits on what a marketplace can promise to users.

A / PROVIDER EVALUATION

The simpler integration wasn't necessarily the workable one.

Razorpay was comparatively straightforward to adopt and offered stronger support in our experience. An HDFC-related constraint regarding the intended fund-handling and escrow arrangement shaped the team's evaluation of Cashfree, despite its more demanding onboarding.

My work included provider research and coordination. This does not establish that an escrow service was implemented in production.

OPTION 01

Razorpay

Easier adoption and support experience

OPERATIONAL CONSTRAINT
OPTION 02

Cashfree

Provider path pursued despite additional onboarding effort

B / MY DIRECT RESPONSIBILITY

Onboarding required more than choosing a gateway.

I worked with accounts and legal teams, coordinated Cashfree applications and submitted required corporate documents including the Memorandum of Association (MOA). I supported verification, provider follow-ups and payment/payout testing.

LEGALACCOUNTS
COORDINATIONOnboardingApplications · MOA · verification
PROVIDERTESTING
C / PAYMENT ≠ PAYOUT

Client payment and designer payout are different responsibilities.

The documented MVP used administrator-triggered bank payouts following applicable approval. Automated payouts and advanced withdrawal logic were later-phase directions, not verified live features.

Client funds→Work reviewed→Admin-triggered payout→Designer
D / COMMERCIAL MODEL ANALYSIS

Pricing needed a workable operating model.

I analyzed commission alternatives alongside provider, verification, payout and relevant tax/accounting considerations. The documented fee model changed after business approval; it does not establish conversion or revenue improvements.

09 / FUNCTIONAL TESTING & CROSS-FUNCTIONAL DELIVERY

Finding a problem was only one part of getting it addressed.

I tested product functionality, documented bugs and potential improvements, raised Plane tickets, participated in stand-ups and worked closely with the Project Manager and development team on follow-up.

B / FROM OBSERVATION TO FOLLOW-UP

A test finding needs a path to action.

Examples included a payment retry dialog remaining visible after cancellation, proposal empty states requiring different recovery messages, and unclear form content. I documented such issues and coordinated next steps rather than claiming to have implemented every fix.

01ObserveReproduce the behavior
02DocumentPlane ticket with context
03DiscussPM · design · development
04Follow upReview status / retest
C–D / DELIVERY COORDINATION

Keeping teams aligned was part of the work.

Through stand-ups and close collaboration with the Project Manager, I clarified dependencies and progress. The broader work crossed the business team, external design studio, developers, QA, accounts, legal and payment providers.

10 / OUTCOMES & REFLECTION

The product experience depends on the decisions behind it.

My role connected product requirements and feedback with commercial research, onboarding, testing, stakeholder coordination and implementation follow-through.

DOCUMENTED CONTRIBUTIONS

What I worked on

Internal-release feedback, UX recommendations, UAT observations, provider onboarding/testing, commission analysis and coordination with PM, business and implementation teams.

VERIFICATION BOUNDARY

What remains unknown

Individual MD approvals, final implementation of proposed dispute and refund-credit rules, later payout automation and exact timing conditions.

NOT MEASURED

What I won't claim

Conversion uplift, reduced disputes, satisfaction gains, payout speed or revenue growth without actual post-launch measurements.

THE TAKEAWAY
A useful product experience depends not only on what users see, but on whether the people, rules and operations behind it can deliver what the interface promises.

Dezinersknot strengthened my ability to connect people, requirements, constraints and delivery — and made clear that small product choices can have significant operational consequences.
